cards.answer: My husband has collected and resold trading cards, collectible toys and watches since he worked at a card shop at 12. For months he was glued to his phone trying to catch limited drops, and he kept losing them to bots. These releases sell out in minutes, and nobody can refresh a dozen stores at once while living their life. So I built Drop Radar over one weekend. The goal was simple: he stops watching his phone, trusts the system to tell him when something matters, and we get that time back together. It is a personal project, and he is its real user.

cards.answer: Drop Radar watches about 40 stores and sources around the clock. That covers store product feeds for new items and restocks, store homepages for a waiting room appearing (a queue going up means a drop is starting), page and keyword watchers, and RSS feeds. Each source has its own check interval, and checks tighten inside the drop windows he knows well, like weekday mornings at one store and evenings at another. Discord restock channels arrive over the official live connection, and an AI deep search hunts for small-batch limited editions the scripted feeds miss.

cards.answer: Drop Radar only pings his phone for what he actually wants: online, at retail price, from the real store. Third-party marketplace sellers are flagged, and in-store sightings, resale listings and giveaways go to the dashboard instead. The same product or link alerts only once per 30 minutes across all sources, and quiet hours keep the night quiet. That filtering came from his feedback. Early alerts were low-value in his judgment, so I moved news and trackers to the dashboard and kept the phone for alerts he can act on.

cards.answer: Drop Radar uses three levels. LIVE means buyable now or the queue is up, and it sends a loud push. SOON is an announcement, with a normal push. INFO goes to the dashboard only. Alerts go to a Telegram bot, with optional Pushover critical alerts and ntfy. Each one carries the product, store, price, seller, when it was posted, when it was seen, and the direct store link. The system pings his phone within seconds of a release going live, and he still makes every purchase himself.

cards.answer: Because no store permits automated checkout, I built the legitimate speed-ups. Drop Radar generates one-tap cart links that open checkout with the item already in the cart. It builds the link and never opens it. It sends reminders 24 hours and 15 minutes before an announced drop, with time zones converted and tested across a daylight-saving change. It also keeps a per-store checklist so his accounts are ready for invite and raffle programs. Every one of these is something he can use without putting his accounts at risk.

cards.answer: Drop Radar reads a dedicated inbox, read-only, every 15 minutes. It parses order, shipping, delivery and cancellation emails from about 15 retailers, plus eBay seller emails. From those it keeps cost basis, what he still holds, going rates with their source and date, days held, and a SELL NOW, HOLD or WATCH suggestion with its reason. For eBay it works out fees, payout and profit, and reminds him 24 and 4 hours before a ship-by deadline. Emails it cannot read go to a review list, never dropped. All of it stays on our home PC.

cards.answer: The Telegram bot is a two-way line to an AI agent, not only an alert channel. Commands like /add, /remove, /status, /remind, /ledger and /price run straight away. Anything else he sends, a text, a dictated note or a screenshot, is saved as feedback. A file watcher notices the new note and queues an agent run. That is the design choice I like most: he talks to the system the way he talks to anyone, and he never has to learn a configuration format or touch a line of code.

cards.answer: A file watcher notices a new note, or a source that has started failing, and queues a run of a dedicated Claude Code agent through an autonomous job queue. The agent has written rules and a living knowledge file. It reads the note, works out what is wrong, edits the code or the source list, runs the tests, restarts the service, and replies on Telegram with what it changed. He never touches a line of code. The tests are the gate between an edit and a restart, which is what makes it reasonable to let an agent change a live system.

cards.answer: The agent also runs on a schedule: a daily review, a weekly review, a weekly resale-picks briefing and a monthly research pass. Every weekly review ends with a feedback check-in. Each change from that week gets Keep, Change and Drop buttons, plus one open question that rotates. He asked for it to be easy, so questions come as tap-to-choose Telegram buttons rather than paragraphs. Every choice is saved to a file the agent acts on and can be undone, and each extra feature has a live on and off switch, so anything he declines comes out without a restart.

cards.answer: Drop Radar is about 3,300 lines of standard-library Python in 12 modules, with no frameworks and no proxies. It uses urllib, sqlite3, imaplib, email, threading and http.server, plus a websocket client I built on ssl and socket. Windows Task Scheduler runs it, with a wrapper that restarts it if it stops. I chose the standard library so there is nothing to install beyond Python and nothing for a dependency update to break on a home PC that has to stay up around the clock. The trade-off is writing small pieces, like the websocket client, myself.

cards.answer: I joined nine community restock servers for him and followed six of their announcement channels into his own private server, where a read-only bot reads the posts. It started as REST polling every 10 seconds. I moved it to Discord's official Gateway through a websocket client written on the standard library, with heartbeat, resume and dead-connection detection, so posts now arrive in about a second, with REST polling as an automatic fallback. There are no self-bots and no user tokens, so it stays inside Discord's rules.

cards.answer: Every Drop Radar source has a health row with real states. The Discord feed counts as healthy only when a followed post actually arrived in the last 24 hours, not just because the code ran. A source that runs without errors but never delivers anything is broken, so health checks for real arrivals. An arrival log records every alert's upstream post time, detection time and send time. It feeds a monthly summary of which sources are fastest and each store's busiest day and hour.

cards.answer: Four bugs showed up only in live data, and all four were fixed. A backoff froze the whole loop for up to an hour, so a blocked host is now skipped, not slept on. Channels with no baseline yet had their first posts swallowed. A substring match let atc fire on watch. And a feedback watcher queued notes it had already handled. None of them appeared in the 25 automated tests, which run on fabricated data. They are the reason health now checks for real arrivals.

cards.answer: Scripted feeds wait for a store to post, so I added an AI deep search to hunt for small-batch limited editions they miss. It uses Claude web research. Its first test run surfaced a limited-edition watch, only 100 made, that sold out within minutes, and my husband got one. That find changed the design: the deep search is now weighted toward limited editions, which he named as his top priority. How often it runs is one of the choices he sets through the tap-to-choose buttons.

cards.answer: Drop Radar has 25 automated tests, all on fabricated data, using unittest. His real data stays home: every purchase, sale and timing record lives on our home PC and never goes into the code repository. Git ignores it twice over, and a test proves it. The public showcase on GitHub Pages is separate from the running system. I treat privacy as something to test rather than trust, because a stray commit of purchase records would be hard to undo.

cards.answer: Before building, I researched all 22 stores he buys from: the platform, the bot protection I could observe, and their terms of service, quoted and dated. None permits automated checkout. TCGplayer and eBay forbid scraping, and eBay's sold-price API is restricted, so going rates are automated only through a paid API that permits it and otherwise flagged for him to check by hand. When a store answers with a 403 or 429, Drop Radar checks it less often, hosts are spaced out, and it never hides behind proxies.

cards.answer: Drop Radar only ever alerts. It never buys, never joins or skips a queue, never solves a CAPTCHA and never tries to get around bot protection, and it uses no proxies. He still makes every purchase himself. I drew that line after reading the terms of all 22 stores: none permits automated checkout. The gain is on the speed side, with alerts in seconds, cart links and reminders, and the trade-off is that a bot would be faster at the final click.

cards.answer: Version 1 went live October 22, 2026 with the store feed, waiting-room, page and RSS watchers, Telegram, Pushover and ntfy alerts, bot commands, a dashboard, drop windows, reminders, feedback notes, and 14 more sources the same day. October 22 to 23 brought a quality reset, daily agent reviews and the Discord reader. October 23 to 24 fixed the loop-freeze and feedback-watcher bugs, added tap-to-choose buttons, and started the deep search, whose first run found the 100-piece watch. October 25 added nine Discord servers, retail-price-only filtering, checkout research on 22 stores, the ledger, the Gateway, cart links, reminders, the arrival log and the weekly check-in.

cards.answer: The evidence is honest but small. The documented win is one find: a 100-piece watch the deep search surfaced in its first run, which he bought. The other numbers describe the build and the plumbing: about 40 sources, about a second from Discord, live since October 22, 2026, and 25 tests on fabricated data.
